Heading: Russian bombing of Ukrainian aid centre kills 26 people
DNU Summary: The strikes destroyed a school used for aid distribution in Komyshuvakha and injured five people.
Body:
Ukraine’s president calls attack in Zaporizhia further proof that Russia does not want any ‌kind of de-escalation or justice.

A Russian ⁠bomb attack on an aid centre in Ukraine has killed 26 people, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said, two more than were reported earlier by Ukraine’s emergency services.

The strikes destroyed a school used as a humanitarian aid distribution centre in the village of Komyshuvakha in the southeastern region of Zaporizhia, Zelenskyy said on Monday. Five other people are reported to have been injured.

“After the first air strike, there was a repeat strike with nine more bombs, ⁠directly on the shelter ⁠where people were gathered,” Ukraine’s president wrote on Telegram.

“The Russians could not have been unaware that ⁠every week residents who have remained in ⁠Komyshuvakha were receiving assistance ⁠aid right there. This is yet further proof that Russia does not want any ‌kind of de-escalation, any real justice.”

Footage posted by Ukrainian emergency services showed a building reduced to piles of smouldering rubble. Rescuers were shown working at the site.

Among those killed were a police officer and two State Emergency Service rescuers, regional Governor Mykhailo Semikin reported on Telegram.

Efforts to rescue people on Monday evening were hindered as Russian drones launched additional attacks in the area that had been bombed, according to Mykhailo Semikin, a military official in Zaporizhia.

“After the humanitarian operation in Oleshky, there was a moment when the next steps could have shown that progress toward peace was possible,” Zelenskyy said on social media. “With these killings, Russia is sending an entirely opposite signal: Russia is counting on more killings.”

Elsewhere in Ukraine, emergency services reported that drone strikes injured 12 people in the eastern Kharkiv region and damaged a refrigeration facility, greenhouses and residential buildings.

Five people were also reported injured in the Black Sea port city of Odesa, where a warehouse was targeted and homes were damaged.

Russia’s Ministry of Defence said that it shot down 212 Ukrainian drones overnight, while the head of Russia’s Samara region, Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev, reported local air defences had repelled an aerial attack, without giving further details.

Heading: Fighting returns to Kherson region after longest Ukraine war ceasefire
DNU Summary: The six-day pause let hundreds leave Russian-occupied Oleshky before strikes resumed Monday.
Body:
Fighting has resumed in Ukraine's Kherson after a six-day truce brought quiet to the front-line region for the first time in years.

The ceasefire - the longest since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022 - allowed hundreds of people trapped in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky and its surroundings to be evacuated.

On Monday morning, local authorities confirmed that strikes had resumed, saying Moscow had hit a medical facility in Kherson city centre. They also said a 62-year-old woman and a 73-year-old man were injured when a Russian drone attacked the car they were travelling in.

Ukraine also accused Russian forces of using the humanitarian ceasefire to strengthen their military positions, rotate units and deliver ammunition.

"The enemy used the humanitarian pause to set up their positions," said Ukraine's General Staff, adding they had recorded rotation of Russian units, expansion of anti-drone equipment on the roads, and delivery of ammunition.

The Kremlin appeared to corroborate this when spokesman Dmitry Peskov said it was "reasonable to assume that the Ukrainian army also used this period for the necessary regrouping".

"It is a completely standard practice in such situations," he added.

The ceasefire had been brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump. Both Kyiv and Moscow thanked her repeatedly, though no details of her involvement were shared.

An unusual show of cooperation came from Russia's human rights ombudsman Yana Lantratova and her Ukrainian counterpart Dmytro Lubinets. The pair oversaw the ceasefire, travelled into Oleshky and were filmed speaking to residents together. They publicly thanked each other for their work, often highlighting that no violations of the ceasefire had been observed.

Both Lantratova and Lubinets called for the initiative to be repeated elsewhere, and Ukraine repeatedly said it would be prepared to observe similar ceasefires on a national level too.

But many have questioned whether this will lead to more cooperation and further truces.

In fact, the Kremlin swiftly dismissed the idea even as the ceasefire was under way, calling Oleshky "an isolated case" which would not affect the "settlement process" – a euphemism for the stalled peace talks. "There are no similar plans or initiatives," Peskov reiterated on Monday.

And although last week the guns fell silent in Kherson region, elsewhere in Ukraine Russia's air strikes continued, killing scores of civilians and destroying crucial infrastructure.

The decision to observe an unusually broad and comparatively lengthy ceasefire in and around Oleshky was therefore a notable exception.

The ceasefire's observance appears, at least in part, to have been linked to Melania Trump's reported involvement. By violating the truce, Moscow would have risked undermining its own efforts to cultivate the crucial relationship with her husband, US President Donald Trump.

Some commentators have argued that Trump himself would be interested in presenting the Oleshky ceasefire as a foreign policy achievement scored days before the US midterm elections on Tuesday.

"I totally get why our official representatives need to 'play along' with the US first lady on Oleshky," said Artyom Sheynin, a prominent figure on Russian state TV.

"I understand why it's so important to create a 'success story' ahead of the elections for the US president, whose wife 'achieved a ceasefire' in Oleshky."

Kyiv, too, had its reasons to be fully compliant. Although relations with the US and its president are often fraught, Ukraine continues to rely heavily on US intelligence and US-made Patriot air defence missiles to counter Russian aerial attacks. Ahead of another tough winter of war, continued American support is essential to protect Ukrainian skies from Russia's assaults.

But though the ceasefire may have been born out of political calculation rather than purely humanitarian compassion, it also resulted in hundreds of civilians escaping.

There were emotional scenes when hundreds of Oleshky residents arrived in northern Ukraine on Saturday. Many were met by tearful relatives they had not seen in years. To the journalists waiting, the evacuees told of years of hunger and hardship in a destroyed town.

The hundreds of residents who decided to stay behind will receive monthly humanitarian aid deliveries, Lantratova said, adding that decision too was the result of Melania Trump's mediation.

Yet the troop rotations and resupply efforts show that neither side is expecting Oleshky to be a blueprint for lasting respite in the future.

As Kherson came under fire again, Ukrainian drones hit several energy facilities across four Russian regions. In Samara, residents reported hearing explosions and seeing black plumes of smoke rising into the sky as an oil refinery was hit for the fifth time in a month.

If the truce brought a rare moment of relief to Oleshky, it has done little to alter the wider trajectory of a war that grinds on for now.

Heading: Zelensky warns Russia could exploit US midterms to launch massive attack
DNU Summary: Zelenskyy said the expected strike would target energy and logistics while US attention focused on the midterm elections.
Body:
by Mira Bhakta 11/02/26 04:35 PM ET

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky warned Russia could use Tuesday’s midterm elections in the U.S. to launch a massive attack against Ukraine.

“We have intel that Russia is preparing a new massive attack on our country – primarily targeting energy and logistics,” he wrote in a statement on social media. “The assumption is basically that tomorrow the world will be watching the American midterms, and what is happening here in Ukraine, along with our difficulties with air defense and Patriot missiles, will be overlooked.”

He renewed his calls for the U.S. and other countries to make Russia “feel that terror is no good,” adding “we must not play games with Russia’s oil or gas revenue.”

“We must put pressure on Russia in such a way that it has no alternative but to end this war. America can do this,” he concluded.

The statement appeared alongside a video of Zelensky describing recent Russian attacks on a humanitarian site in Ukraine that reportedly killed 34 people, with some victims still stuck under the rubble.

He added that air raid sirens were playing in Kyiv as the city braces for potential missile fire.

This comes after first lady Melania Trump announced a localized ceasefire between the European countries in and around Oleshky — a town occupied by Russia since its invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Ukrainian officials accused Russia of using the ceasefire to bring in new troops, strengthen its military positions, add in more antidrone defenses on roads and send more ammunition to the area, according to multiple outlets.

The ceasefire ended on Sunday, with the first lady calling it a “success,” touting on social media that it enabled “the evacuation of nearly 800 people.”

Three-way peace negotiations between the U.S., Ukraine and Russia are slated for later this month in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates.

Heading: Iran says it can reopen Hormuz in two days if US meets conditions
DNU Summary: Tehran wants sanctions lifted, frozen assets released and the US naval blockade ended.
Body:
Iran said on Monday it was ready to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if the US accepted its conditions, having proposed a seven-day timeline when it first put the idea to Washington through Qatar in September.

"The possibility of implementing this plan in two days is another indication of Iran's good-faith approach," foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said.

"We have stated that, if Iran's demands are met, it would be possible to restore security to the Strait of Hormuz and resume the negotiating process within a short period," he added.

Baghaei said that an exchange of messages was ongoing with the US via mediators and that "everything depends" on the US side accepting Iran's demands. "Only then can we discuss the subsequent stages," he explained.

Tehran's conditions include ending the war on all fronts, unfreezing Iranian assets abroad, lifting sanctions on its oil sector, and ending the US naval blockade of Iranian ports.

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi set out further requirements in an Al Jazeera interview released on Sunday, saying Washington must also accept a new transit route through the strait agreed between Iran and Oman, reduce US troop numbers in the region, and remove sanctions imposed since August.

Washington has rolled out a fresh wave of measures from August onwards, which it described as the "economic asphyxiation" of Iran.

Since the Iran war broke out in late February, Tehran has claimed it maintained control over Hormuz, regularly targeting vessels that attempt to cross without its authorisation. Meanwhile, the US imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports.

The diplomatic activity comes as both Washington and Tel Aviv have intensified military threats. On Saturday, Trump said he still had to "take care" of one or two targets, including Pickaxe mountain in central Iran, a site Washington suspects houses nuclear infrastructure, which Tehran denies.

Baghaei warned at Monday's briefing that "any act of aggression against Iran, any military attack against Iran, by whatever means, will be met with a powerful, immediate and comprehensive response from us."

Iran's deputy foreign minister Kazem Gharibabadi travelled to Doha on Monday to help draft a preliminary agreement, with Qatar acting as mediator.

China said it was sending its special envoy Zhai Jun to Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia to press all sides to halt the fighting. President Xi Jinping said the Middle East and Gulf must not become an arena for great-power competition. Beijing and Muscat jointly called on Washington and Tehran to return to the "Islamabad memorandum of understanding," Chinese state media reported.

Officials in Tehran continued to set red lines. Deputy parliament speaker Ali Nikzad said Iran would not enter nuclear negotiations under pressure, and that previous talks had produced only broken promises.

Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said on Saturday that the US would need to meet Iran's conditions before talks could begin. Rezaei said he had received a letter from US Vice President JD Vance but had not yet replied.

US military command CENTCOM rejected Iranian claims that its strikes had targeted only military objectives. CENTCOM said on X that Iran had deliberately hit residential areas, civilian centres and civilian sailors in international waters, and that its attacks had killed at least 20 people.

Anwar Gargash, adviser to the UAE president, told the Manama Dialogue conference in Bahrain that Abu Dhabi did not want a prolonged crisis with Iran but acknowledged that trust had been lost. "This damage was not caused by us. Rather, following Iran's attack on us, trust was damaged," he said.

The diplomatic activity falls ahead of US midterm elections on Tuesday, in which economic pressures linked to the Iran war have increased the likelihood of Republican losses in Congress.

The announcement of results on Wednesday coincides with the anniversary of the 1979 seizure of the US embassy in Tehran, during which 52 US diplomats were held for over a year. Tehran-organised demonstrations against the US are expected across the country, while billboards depicting Trump behind prison bars have been erected in Tehran in recent days.

Trump said on Sunday evening that he and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had held "very good" talks the previous day and discussed Iran, without elaborating. Netanyahu's office has not commented on the meeting.

Since Israeli voters went to the polls last Tuesday, Netanyahu has spoken publicly only about the vote. Results remain inconclusive, with preliminary assessments suggesting he may not secure a coalition, although no alternative government has taken shape.

Heading: Romania and Moldova Seal First Joint Defence Procurement Deal
DNU Summary: The agreement would let neutral Moldova access EU SAFE financing for military vehicles.
Body:
Romania and Moldova signed a military cooperation agreement on Monday, paving the way for the latter to access the European Union’s Security Action for Europe SAFE programme to finance the purchase of military vehicles.

The agreement marks the first joint defence procurement arrangement between the two countries and represents another step towards strengthening their military cooperation, officials said.

“This is a major opportunity for both countries to strengthen their cooperation in the fields of economy and security … and also a good way to protect our territories and our citizens,” Romanian Prime Minister Luca Niculescu said.

He added that SAFE funding would allow both countries to modernise their defence capabilities while supporting the development of Europe’s defence-industrial base through joint procurement.

Although Moldova is not an EU member and its constitution enshrines a policy of neutrality, it can participate in the programme through a partnership with an EU member state, in this case Romania.

Under the agreement, Moldova may join an existing procurement framework between Romania and Italian manufacturer IDV, Iveco Defence Vehicles, allowing it to acquire 62 multipurpose IVECO military trucks.

The vehicles, which will be produced at an IVECO plant in Romania, are intended to replace ageing Soviet-era trucks still in service with Moldova’s armed forces.

Moldovan Defence Minister Anatolie Nosatii said the acquisition would improve the army’s logistical and operational capabilities, while helping align military standards and strengthen interoperability with Romania.

Officials also indicated that Bucharest and Chisinau could extend their cooperation under SAFE to include air-defence and anti-drone technologies.

Both countries face growing security challenges stemming from Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Moldova, which borders Ukraine and lies close to the war-affected Black Sea region, has become concerned about the risks posed by Russian military activity and hybrid operations.

Although constitutionally neutral, Moldova has stepped up efforts to modernise its armed forces and strengthen cooperation with Western partners. Romania, an EU and NATO member sharing a border with Moldova, has been one of its strongest supporters, providing political, economic and security assistance as Chisinau pursues closer integration with the European Union.

The SAFE programme, adopted by the EU in 2025, provides up to €150 billion in loans to member states for joint defence procurement. It is designed to accelerate military investment, strengthen Europe’s defence industry and reduce reliance on non-European suppliers.

The framework also allows eligible non-EU partner countries, including Moldova, to participate in certain joint procurement arrangements.

Heading: Ukraine and Russia both report fake emergency alerts after cyberattacks target apps as limited ceasefire ends
DNU Summary: Ukraine said its service was restored after false nuclear warnings, while Russia reported a separate app breach.
Body:
KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Authorities in Ukraine and Russia said their emergency alert mobile apps had been targeted by cyberattacks, with users in Ukraine receiving false warnings of an imminent nuclear threat.

It was not clear if the attacks late Sunday were related. Ukraine said its service, which residents rely on to seek safety amid daily Russian missile and drone strikes, was up and running again after being suspended due to the attack.

WATCH: Inside a Ukrainian city hit by Russian drones during the Starlink disruption

Russian authorities said Monday that hackers had sent fake emergency alerts after gaining access to the Russian Emergency Situations Ministry's mobile app, and that efforts were ongoing to restore the app's functionality.

A Russian Telegram channel said a hacking group, Hitcore, had claimed responsibility for the breach of the Ukrainian system, but that could not be independently verified. Any affiliations or other details surrounding the identities or motivations of the purported hackers were unclear.

The alerts received by Ukrainians — making false claims of high radiation levels, a chemical threat and public disturbances in Kyiv — were written in English with spelling and grammatical errors as well as in a mix of Russian and Ukrainian.

One of the messages, written in Russian, said: "Hi! There will be a nuclear threat across Ukraine. Do not worry, the Oreshnik is incoming," a reference to a Russian intermediate-range ballistic missile.

In a Telegram post late Sunday following the breach, Ukraine's air raid alert channel said "unauthorized parties" had interfered with the app's operation and warned users not to click on links in "suspicious notifications."

Ukraine's state-run Center for Countering Disinformation urged users to monitor other emergency channels on social media and rely on physical alerts while the cyberattack was being addressed.

Yurii Ihnat, a spokesman for Ukraine's air force command, told Ukraine's private 1+1 television that the cyberattack had no impact on Ukraine's security and defense operations because the app is separate from military command systems.

In a statement, Russia's Emergency Ministry said that hackers had used its mobile app to send a false alert across 33 of Russia's 89 regions at approximately 2:45 a.m. Moscow time (11:45 p.m. GMT). It did not name who it believed carried out the attack.

The ministry said that the digital vulnerability exploited by the attackers had been identified and that "necessary measures" were being taken to prevent a similar breach. It also reassured Russians that the wider public alert system was working normally through SMS messages, media broadcasts and municipal sirens and loudspeakers.

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said that all of Russia's state agencies were under the constant threat of cyberattacks, including a growing number that use artificial intelligence.

"All government bodies must take steps to improve the cybersecurity of our digital resources," Peskov said.

Ukrainian authorities in the war-divided Kherson region reported multiple Russian drone attacks early Monday, hours after a humanitarian ceasefire expired.

The regional administration said a 62-year-old woman and a 73-year-old man were hospitalized with blast injuries in the city of Kherson, across the Dnipro River from Russian-occupied territory.

The localized ceasefire, which began on Oct. 27, ended at midnight at the start of Monday. The brief pause in fighting was part of a humanitarian aid and evacuation mission in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, and marked the most significant truce between Kyiv and Moscow since Russia's full-scale invasion began nearly five years ago.

Speaking to reporters in Kyiv on Monday, Ukraine's ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said the oldest person evacuated to Ukrainian territory during the mission was 94 years old, and added that 104 pets, including four parrots, were also rescued.

Lubinets, who was Ukraine's lead civilian negotiator for the mission, said he hoped the localized ceasefire and evacuation would act as a "pilot model" for other missions, and could "add to the momentum" of three-way negotiations between Ukrainian, Russian and U.S. officials expected this month.

He said Ukraine hoped to make future aid deliveries to residents who chose to stay in Oleshky, and that the delivery mechanism was still being worked out. He described the involvement of U.S. first lady Melania Trump, who helped broker the limited truce, as critical.

"Without the American representation, we could not even imagine such cooperation because many bodies, including military and intelligence, were involved in this combined effort," he said.

Lubinets described the mission as exhausting and "very complicated."

"We crossed into the territory of the Russian Federation and had to remain alert at all times," he said. "We are dog-tired."

An estimated 2,000 civilians were in Oleshky when the temporary truce took effect. They could evacuate to territory controlled by either Ukraine or Russia, or remain in the city with replenished food and medical supplies. Exact evacuation totals were withheld to protect those who stayed.

Ukraine's general staff said Monday that Russia's military had bolstered its drone defenses and replenished ammunition supplies in the area during the ceasefire.

Elsewhere in Ukraine, emergency services reported that drone strikes injured 12 people in the eastern Kharkiv region and damaged a refrigeration facility, greenhouses and residential buildings.

Five people were also reported injured in the Black Sea port city of Odesa, where a warehouse was targeted and homes were damaged.

Russia's Ministry of Defense said Monday that it shot down 212 Ukrainian drones overnight, while the head of Russia's Samara region, Gov. Vyacheslav Fedorishchev, said in a statement that local air defenses were repelling an aerial attack, but did not give further details.

Independent Russian media outlets later reported that Ukrainian drones had targeted one of Europe's largest oil transport hubs in Samara.

Katie Marie Davies contributed to this report from Manchester, England.

Heading: Shop fridges and freezers across Europe hit by fresh suspected cyber-attack
DNU Summary: Retailers in seven countries reported refrigeration systems reaching as high as 50C.
Body:
Supermarket chains in at least seven European countries have said the temperatures of refrigerators and freezers in some of their shops soared overnight to as high as 50C (122F), echoing a cyber-attack last month that caused millions of euros of damage in France.

Retailers in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Finland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden reported problems with their refrigeration systems on Monday, and several companies confirmed they had been hacked.

The EU food and agriculture commissioner, Christophe Hansen, said the repeated cyber-attacks were deeply concerning, calling them “a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumers’ confidence in it”.

The incidents follow an attack in France last month in which hackers seized control of cooling units in as many as 700 supermarkets, raising their temperatures as high ⁠as 50C (122F) and causing fires and food losses estimated in the tens of millions of euros.

A growing range of devices, including refrigeration systems, can now be monitored and controlled remotely, leading authorities to particularly fear government-sponsored hybrid attacks ​in after Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

Sweden’s Coop chain told the daily Aftonbladet that six of ​its shops ‌had been ​hit, while ICA said it was “aware that a limited ​number of stores were affected by an incident overnight which impacted their refrigeration and freezer systems”.

An ICA shop at Sjöbo in southern Sweden posted that its fridges and freezers had been hacked and their temperature set at 50C. Another in Stockholm said its freezers were broken “due to a 2am cyberattack” and that “everything was destroyed”.

The head of Sweden’s national cybersecurity centre, John Billow, said it ‌was working on incidents around the country. It had established the country had “quite a lot of exposed operational ‌technology devices” that needed updating or patching, he told Reuters.

The Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize, which last ​month ​reported a ​similar incident ​to police in the Netherlands, said fridges and ⁠freezers in dozens of its ⁠supermarkets in ​Belgium ‌and ‌Luxembourg had been hit.

It did not specify the cause, but reporters visiting a shop north-east of Brussels saw refrigerators and freezers empty and a sign reading: “Due to cyberattacks, there will be no products on the refrigerated or freezer shelves. We offer our sincere apologies.”

A company spokesperson, Sarah ‌De Meester, said the range of fresh and frozen products was “temporarily somewhat limited” in affected shops, but that distribution centres were operating normally and there was no disruption to deliveries.

Belgium’s Le Soir newspaper reported that dozens of shops and supermarkets had been affected, including five Spar outlets, Shop & Go convenience shops attached to Q8 service stations and some smaller Proxy Delhaize mini-markets.

“We started mobilising technicians at 1am,” Stephan Moelans, the chief executive of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize’s refrigeration systems, told the paper. “We spent all night and morning disconnecting the affected installations.”

He told the Belga news agency the ‌incident had been a cyber-attack and that the units’ evaporators were switched to defrost mode.

The Colruyt and Intermarché supermarket chains also said they had been hit by technical problems affecting fridges in five and 15 of their shops respectively, and Carrefour Belgium reported disruption in about 15 of its 700 shops.

“It’s a cyber-attack, there is no other reason,” said Mich Vergauwen, a Carrefour spokesperson. An Ikea Belgium spokesperson likewise told Agence France-Presse that a cyber-attack had caused the temperature of freezers in its Mons shop to rise suddenly.

Ikea, famous for its in-store Swedish meatballs, said it had had to ‌remove some food products from refrigeration units ​as a precaution and expected some food waste as ⁠a result.

In Finland, the Helsingin Sanomat newspaper said shops operated by the Kesko supermarket chain were investigating similar problems, while the Dutch public radio NOS reported that the systems of at least 17 mainly small local shops had been affected.

At one Estonian supermarket chain, attackers accessed a computer controlling the refrigeration system and turned up the temperature to 50C, the refrigeration supply company Kitman Coldtech told the ERR broadcaster.

“This is very fresh, it happened this morning,” its chief executive, Jann Mutso, said, adding that the attack was responded to within minutes and there had been no significant damage. The Selver supermarket chain said one of its outlets had been affected.

Ireland’s third-largest supermarket ⁠chain, ⁠SuperValu, said ​refrigeration systems limited ⁠to ​a ‌specific ‌model ‌in 13 of its 223 shops ‌had been affected by ​a cyber-incident, ⁠and that chilled and ​frozen products ​had been removed from ​sale.

Many cyber-attacks involve extortion or are politically motivated and are potentially carried out by state-level actors, said Tom Hegel of the cybersecurity firm SentinelOne. But the supermarket attacks, with no financial demands, point to sabotage, he said.

“Retail is an easy target because retail chains run enormous estates of refrigeration controllers, building management systems, door access panels and point-of-sale gear,” Hegel told Reuters.

Patrick Lamplmair of the cybersecurity firm Tributech said cyber-attackers would keep going “until it stops working” because the method was “cheap and the damage is immediate”. Many refrigeration systems had known and as yet unfixed flaws, he said.

“Thousands of these controllers were still reachable from the internet after the French attack,” he added. “A few commands to a temperature controller can destroy stock overnight and close stores.”

In the French attack, the hackers pirated controllers mostly supplied by the Danish company Danfoss, which said subsequently that it had identified some security flaws last year and had “long recommended” customers install updates.

The hackers remotely overrode the settings on thousands of freezers, fridges and chiller cabinets at chains including Intermarché, Coopérative U, Carrefour, Leclerc and Monoprix, pushing them from as low as -27C to well over 50C.

The shops had to discard vast quantities of fresh meat, dairy and frozen products. Individual supermarkets reportedly suffered losses ranging from tens of thousands of euros to more than €130,000 (£109,000).

The Paris prosecutor’s office has opened a formal investigation into the French attack and the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, instructed France’s national cybersecurity agency, Ansii, to investigate.

The agency subsequently reported that supermarkets using controllers from two other companies had also been targeted in the attack, but authorities have not indicated who could have been behind the incidents. There have been no claims of responsibility.

Heading: Bulgaria’s Presidential Election Winner Pledges Reset with Russia
DNU Summary: Iliana Iotova won 57.6% of the runoff vote amid turnout of 29.1%.
Body:
Bulgaria’s acting President, Iliana Iotova, cemented a five-year mandate after winning the runoff election on Sunday. Backed by the Progressive Bulgaria government and her former Bulgarian Socialist Party, BSP, Iotova won 57.6 per cent of votes cast against the pro-EU opposition candidate, Andrey Gyurov, on 39.5 per cent. Turnout was low at 29.1 per cent, but higher than the all-time low of 22.98 per cent registered in the first round on October 25.

“People believed in our way of politics, which pledged dialogue, conversations, searching for decisions, coordination,” Iotova said on Sunday evening in a briefing that Prime Minister Rumen Radev also attended and where he answered most of the questions.

“Bulgarians chose the future instead of the past, they chose peace, stability, normalcy”, said Radev, both of them dodging questions on the low turnout.

Iotova built her campaign as “the President of peace”: she has pledged to offer a more balanced attitude towards Russia and be skeptical about further military aid to Ukraine. She has also called for Bulgaria to be less obedient to the EU.

“If you say yes to everything, which was Bulgaria’s case for decades, you are voiceless … but things have changed a lot, times have changed in the EU, too”, Iotova said in a TV debate with Andrey Gyurov.

In an interview on October 30 on YouTube with two pro-Russian commentators, she said: “I don’t see Russia as an enemy state … I hope Russia will take part in Europe’s future security architecture.”

During her campaign, Iotova was criticised, along with Prime Minister and Progressive Bulgaria leader Rumen Radev, for remaining elusive about drone attacks in the Black Sea, including in Bulgaria’s zone, and for a lack of preparedness.

Her Vice will be Kiril Valchev, Director of the Bulgarian News Agency, the country’s official newswire, his nomination raising questions about Bulgaria’s media freedom and political ties.

After her victory on Sunday, Iotova said all the criticism from the opposition had been a form of aggressive political attacking, adding: “But we didn’t allow ourselves this speech of hate.”

Iotova was born in 1964 in Sofia. She worked as a TV presenter and news editor at Bulgarian National Television in the 1990s. Her time there is remembered for a controversy from 1995, when, on air, she prioritized coverage of then-Socialist Prime Minister Zhan Videnov doing a traditional dance, or horo, at a public event instead of covering the death of 14 soldiers during an accident – the case became colloquially known as “the blood horo”.

Iotova’s involvement with the Moscow-aligned Bulgarian Socialist Party started in 1997, first as a head of the party’s press office. She joined the party аs Bulgaria was going through an economic crisis and was pressured by mass protests aimed at Socialist-led cabinets.

Iotova became an MP in 2005, when the BSP clung to power through a coalition with the NDSV, the National Movement for Stability and Progress, the now faded party of former monarch Simeon Saxe-Coburg-Gotha.

She became a Member of the European Parliament in 2007 and again in 2014.

In 2016, she resigned from the EP to become a Vice President when Rumen Radev won his first term.

She remained in position until January 2026 when, following months of speculation, Radev resigned from the Presidency to form his own party, Progressive Bulgaria, which won the April elections. This made Iotova acting President, while Radev became the first politician to have served both as President and Prime Minister.

Heading: France launches attempted murder investigation after petrol bomb thrown at police
DNU Summary: An officer suffered ankle burns during Saturday’s largely peaceful nationwide protests.
Body:
Prosecutors in France have launched an attempted murder investigation after petrol bombs were thrown at police during unrest, French media reported.

An image of a police officer with his leg on fire during a clash with protesters in Paris on Saturday has prompted outrage and follows weeks of street protests in France that have also seen demonstrators injured.

The officer, who suffered burns to his ankle and minor injures to his hand, told French newspaper Le Figaro it was a "particularly sophisticated" incendiary device.

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said throwing a molotov cocktail at a police line was "what I call a murder attempt", adding officers were working to find the perpetrators.

Hundreds of thousands of people demonstrated across France in largely peaceful protests on Saturday, the latest in a series of youth-led protests that began in late September demanding action on the high cost of living and poor public services, especially schools.

Following previous clashes and looting, thousands of police officers were deployed across the country over the weekend, and officers fired tear gas at demonstrators in some cities.

There were more than 770 arrests on Saturday, roughly half as many as the previous week's protests, the French interior ministry said.

But police said no one had been arrested for the attack caught on camera that set a police officer on fire, AFP reported.

The officer - part of the National Gendarmerie, a national law enforcement force that is technically part of the military but under the control of the interior ministry - said his unit "suddenly found ourselves facing several hundred hostile, well equipped adversaries".

Speaking to French newspaper Le Figaro, he said police were yet to identify the liquid used but that the incendiary device "had a far greater burning capacity than a standard Molotov cocktail".

"We faced hostile individuals who are not protesters," he said. "These adversaries are there with the intent to harm those who represent the state."

Fourteen other officers sustained wounds ranging from minor to serious, he said, adding some were struck by paving stones. The unit was supposed to be on leave but had been urgently recalled to police the weekend protests, he said.

French protest organisers, the Gilets Jaunes, or Yellow Vests, have said dozens of protesters have been seriously injured during recent demonstrations across the country, with many hurt by "grenades".

France suspended the use of one type of stun grenade while policing student protests in early October after a 15-year-old's hand was blown off, but French newspaper Le Monde has reported that police have continued to use a different model in subsequent protests.

Protests also took place in Germany and Italy over the weekend, as mainly youth-led protests continue across parts of Europe, with varying demands but broadly linked to a focus on cost-of-living issues and public services.

Heading: Poland’s Rule-of-Law Crisis Deepens as Rival Judges Claim Control of Top Court
DNU Summary: A judge blocked from taking office called a Tuesday assembly to approve the court’s 2027 budget.
Body:
A decade-long dispute over who controls Poland’s highest court escalated over the weekend, when a group of judges sought to remove its leadership, police were deployed to the building, and President Karol Nawrocki cut short a foreign trip to intervene.

The next flashpoint is seen on Tuesday, November 3, when Anna Korwin-Piotrowska – one of the five judges elected by the current parliamentary majority but prevented from taking up their duties by the country’s president – has called a general assembly of Constitutional Tribunal judges to approve the court’s proposed budget for 2027. With the existing leadership, led by the court’s president Bogdan Swieczkowski, continuing to dispute her authority, it remains unclear whether the meeting can proceed as planned.

The battle over the makeup of the Constitutional Tribunal, which has the power to overturn laws that violate Poland’s constitution and should act as an independent check on government and parliament, dates back to 2015, when both the outgoing centrist government and its right-wing successor made contested appointments to it. During Law and Justice’s (PiS) subsequent eight years in power, major reforms to the judiciary raised concerns over political interference and brought Poland into prolonged conflict with European institutions over the state of the rule of law in the country.

Reversing those reforms was among Donald Tusk’s central campaign promises before his coalition took office in 2023 and his pro-European government has made restoring the court’s independence an essential part of repairing the country’s democratic institutions. The Tusk-led government has since refused to recognise the Tribunal’s legitimacy in its current form, but attempts to change the system through legislation have been blocked by opposition-aligned presidents.

The immediate deadlock concerns five judges elected by the current parliament whom Nawrocki has refused to swear in. These judges subsequently took their oaths without him, but the Tribunal’s leadership prevented them from hearing cases. In October, the Venice Commission, the Council of Europe’s constitutional advisory body, concluded that the president could not use his role in the appointment process to obstruct duly elected judges from taking office.

However, PiS and President Nawrocki accuse Tusk of using unlawful methods to replace the court’s leadership with judges sympathetic to his government.

The competing claims came to a head on Friday, when the five judges attempted to assert their authority over the Tribunal. Korwin-Piotrowska announced the suspension of its president, Swieczkowski, and his deputy, and declared herself the court’s acting head. The existing leadership rejected the move, leaving the institution with rival claims to authority.

Separately, Justice Minister Waldemar Zurek sought to have Swieczkowski and his deputy, Bartlomiej Sochanski, stripped of judicial immunity, potentially paving the way for criminal charges over their alleged obstruction of the Tribunal’s work.

The announcement brought more protesters to the Tribunal’s grounds in Warsaw, where supporters of the opposition had already been demonstrating for weeks against attempts by the newly elected judges to take up their posts. Senior PiS politicians joined the crowd, while police increased their presence around the building.

Meanwhile, President Nawrocki cut short a state visit to Senegal, ordering his plane to turn around over Spain and return to Warsaw. He arrived at the Tribunal in the early hours of Saturday, challenged the authority of the judges seeking to take control, and helped the court’s deputy president enter the building.

“Last night, Poland’s constitutional order was violated, and a constitutional state institution was forcibly taken over,” Nawrocki said in a statement issued shortly after 05:00 on Saturday morning. He demanded that police withdraw from the premises and announced emergency consultations with parliamentary party leaders.

In a televised address on Saturday evening, Prime Minister Tusk defended the intervention, accusing PiS and the PiS-aligned presidents Andrzej Duda and his successor Nawrocki of perpetuating the crisis. “Nobody had any doubt that the Tribunal, in the form imposed by PiS, was not a real court,” he said, arguing that repeated attempts to resolve the dispute through legislation had been blocked.

Tusk compared the situation to a thief who steals an elderly woman’s handbag, then complains of violence when caught, while bystanders suggest dividing the stolen money between the thief and the victim. “On certain matters, there can be no compromise,” he said.

A constitutional reset to end an undignified row?

Poland’s Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights, a leading civil liberties organisation, questioned whether Friday’s intervention by the government would help restore the Tribunal’s authority, calling the escalation “extremely harmful”.

“The confrontations between judges and the President of the Republic of Poland outside the entrance to the Tribunal building undermine the dignity and authority of state institutions,” the organisation said in a statement.

The European Commission weighed in on Saturday, backing the Polish parliament’s authority to appoint Tribunal judges. Meanwhile, US Ambassador Tom Rose warned that crowds outside the court risked worsening an already volatile situation. “The last thing Poland needs is a confrontation that spirals out of control,” he wrote on X, while stressing that Washington did not intend to interfere in Poland’s domestic affairs.

With parliamentary elections scheduled for 2027, Tusk’s coalition faces pressure to deliver on its promise to restore judicial independence, while the opposition has made resistance to the government’s intervention a central issue. In August, Tusk announced that he was determined to ensure the newly elected judges could take up their posts at the Tribunal by September, even if the process was not particularly elegant. Speaking at the Campus Polska Przyszlosci event, he said he needed to be certain that “our judges will enter that building”.

On Saturday afternoon, Nawrocki held meetings with parliamentary party leaders to discuss possible solutions. Among the proposals put forward by parties as far apart as the left-wing Razem and the far-right Confederation was a constitutional reset of the Tribunal, involving the replacement of all its sitting judges with a new bench appointed through a cross-party agreement.

Heading: Russia Officially Withdraws From Europe’s Anti-Torture Convention
DNU Summary: Council of Europe inspectors had visited more than 450 Russian detention facilities before the treaty withdrawal.
Body:
Independent international monitoring of detention facilities in Russia has come to an end with the country’s formal withdrawal from the European Convention for the Prevention of Torture, the Council of Europe said on Sunday.

In a statement, the Council of Europe said inspectors from the convention had carried out 30 visits to more than 450 detention facilities in Russia during the 23 years it was a member. Russia, however, permitted the publication of only four visit reports over that period.

“Russia may authorize the publication of [the remaining] reports at any time,” the statement read, noting that the unpublished reports relate to 10 visits to the republic of Chechnya and the remaining North Caucasus regions between 2000 and 2017.

Per convention rules, Russia’s withdrawal took effect on Nov. 1, one year after Moscow formally notified the Council of Europe of its decision.

Russia ratified the anti-torture treaty in 1998, two years after joining the Council of Europe. It was expelled from the Council of Europe in March 2022 following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The Council of Europe said the convention received “numerous accounts of alleged acts of torture and ill-treatment” across detention centers and penal colonies in Russian-occupied Ukraine and within Russia itself.

“However, due to the non-cooperation of the Russian authorities, the CPT has been unable to conduct a visit to the Russian Federation to examine the situation for itself,” it said.

Russia also withdrew from the European Convention on Human Rights in 2022, ending its jurisdiction under the European Court of Human Rights.

Rights groups have warned that exiting the treaty removes the last remaining international safeguard for inmates in Russia’s penal system. They have credited the convention for helping to ease overcrowding, improving conditions in penal colonies and securing better protection for some inmates.

Russia remains a party to the UN Convention Against Torture, which it ratified in 1985.

Heading: Ukrainian Drones Hit Major Oil Transport Hub in Samara Region
DNU Summary: Authorities confirmed an air raid, while satellite imagery showed smoke near Transneft’s station.
Body:
Ukrainian drones struck one of Europe’s largest oil transport hubs in Russia’s Samara region, independent media reported Monday, as local authorities confirmed the overnight attack in the southern region without detailing any damage or casualties.

Samara region Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said early Monday that air defense systems were repelling an air barrage and urged residents not to post photos or videos online.

Samara’s Kurumoch International Airport temporarily suspended flights for two hours during the air raid alert.

The exiled news outlet Astra said it used eyewitness photos of a smoke cloud in Samara to identify at least one targeted facility as Transneft’s linear production and dispatch station. NASA satellite imagery also showed a large, black plume of smoke rising in the area where the site is located, directly southeast of the regional capital.

The Transneft station spans 216 hectares (534 acres) and has 71 storage tanks with a total capacity of 1.6 million cubic meters. It receives crude from Western Siberia, the republic of Tatarstan, the Orenburg region and Kazakhstan via four pipelines before routing it toward two refineries and the Druzhba export pipeline.

Monday’s attack marks the fifth drone strike on the Transneft production and dispatch station after reported strikes on Oct. 2, 7, 10 and 11.

It also came as Russia’s Emergency Situations Ministry said a major cyberattack targeted the app it uses to send people warnings about incoming air attacks. Ukraine reported a similar cyberattack on its air raid alert system earlier in the day, which it said sent out false messages about a radiation threat.

Russia’s Defense Ministry said it intercepted 212 Ukrainian drones across Russia and annexed Crimea between Sunday evening and Monday morning. Authorities in the Belgorod, Voronezh and Rostov regions reported minor damage and injuries.

In an interview with state TV channel Vesti on Sunday, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak, who oversees Russia’s energy sector, said Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries were adding to global fuel market imbalances and affecting prices.

That same day, Nizhny Novgorod region Governor Gleb Nikitin said a large-scale Ukrainian drone caused “significant damage” to an industrial facility. He did not identify the site that was hit. The region is home to the NORSI oil refinery, one of Russia’s largest.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky also said Sunday that his armed forces had hit the Kamensky plant in Russia’s Rostov region, which he said was involved in the manufacture of Russian missiles.

Despite U.S. attempts last month to introduce an energy ceasefire in the war, which is now approaching its fifth anniversary, Russia and Ukraine have continued to target power grid infrastructure, as well as oil refineries and other facilities.

In an interview with Fox News on Sunday, Zelensky reiterated his position that Ukraine will halt its attacks on Russian refineries if Moscow also puts an end to its strikes on the Ukrainian electrical grid.

Heading: Kremlin Downplays Prospect of Resuming Gas Shipments to Europe via Ukraine
DNU Summary: A proposed winter energy ceasefire reportedly included restoring transit through Ukraine with proceeds held in escrow.
Body:
Russia is unlikely to resume natural gas deliveries to Europe via Ukrainian pipelines anytime soon, the Kremlin said Monday, downplaying reports that the option was being discussed as part of a proposed winter energy ceasefire.

The Wall Street Journal reported earlier that the Trump administration suggested the idea during talks in September as an incentive for Moscow to halt strikes on Ukraine’s energy grid. According to U.S. and European officials, advocates of the plan argued it would also allow Ukraine to collect transit fees while helping lower European heating costs.

Under the proposal, Russian gas would be sold through a U.S. intermediary to navigate European sanctions, with proceeds placed in an offshore escrow account to prevent Moscow from using the funds to finance its war effort.

“Frankly, the situation on the ground speaks all too clearly to the fact that those kinds of plans are impossible to implement right now,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters during a daily briefing. “But as for what the future holds, we’ll see.”

Peskov said any renewal of gas shipments through Ukraine would “depend on the willingness of buyers, the willingness of sellers and the capacity of sellers.”

He noted that, while the European energy market remains a “premium one,” countries in the Global South have demonstrated themselves as “centers of economic growth,” meaning that their consumption of oil and gas will only increase in the coming years, with Moscow poised to supply all of their energy needs.

Russian gas shipments to Europe by pipeline have largely stopped since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and Brussels has committed to ending all imports of Russian oil and gas by the end of 2027.

According to the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis, a U.S.-based think tank, the EU imported 6.9 billion cubic meters of Russian gas in the first three months of 2026, a 16% increase from the first quarter of last year and the highest volume since 2022.

Still, Russia now accounts for just 11% of Europe’s natural gas consumption, down from 45% on the eve of the 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

Heading: Human rights group: at least 69 political prisoners in Russian custody have died since February 2022
DNU Summary: Memorial linked many of the deaths to illness and inadequate medical care in detention.
Body:
Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Russian article.

A Russian human rights group says at least 69 people subjected to political persecution have died in Russia or Russian-occupied territory since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022.

Speaking on the eve of Russia's Day of Remembrance for Victims of Political Repression, Sergei Davidis, head of the "Political Prisoners. Memorial" human rights project, said the most common cause of death was from illness and lack of medical care.

According to Davidis, the team has been compiling lists of political prisoners and monitoring political repression since 2008: 81 people whose imprisonment was politically motivated died during that time. "Of those," Davidis said, "69 died after the start of the full-scale war. The increase is enormous."

While Russian officials have not commented on this specific report, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, as recently as September, has denied reports that Russia holds political prisoners.

Davidis said since the war began, the numbers have increased substantially.

"When we began monitoring the situation, there were about 30 people on our list. Today, the number of political prisoners exceeded 1,800," he said.

He also said repression has become more severe.

"When we first began monitoring the situation, torture was not as widespread as it is now, for example, in cases involving Ukrainian citizens," Davidis said.

The longtime human rights advocate said deaths from illness and the denial or delayed provision of medical care have become a systemic problem. The report also states that "increasing numbers of young people, including minors, are being subjected to politically motivated imprisonment."

Davidis said political repression in Russia is not some isolated phenomenon carried out by judges or individual security officers.

"The brutality of this repression and the absence of any leniency toward prisoners are deliberate state policies, not simply individual abuses by officials," he said. "Those directly involved in the deaths of specific political prisoners bear responsibility and must be held accountable."

Heading: Trump says aides have ‘concept’ of Canada trade deal
DNU Summary: Trump and Prime Minister Mark Carney discussed the deal Saturday after months of reciprocal tariffs.
Body:
President Trump said Sunday his administration and Canadian officials are close to reaching a deal to end their months-long trade dispute.

“We have the concept of a very good deal with Canada,” Trump told reporters in Iowa, adding the two sides are “very close” to reaching an agreement.

The president noted he spoke to Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Saturday, saying the deal they discussed would be “great for our farmers, great for our country” and “fine” for Canada.

“Part of the agreement is that our farmers will have to pay no tariffs,” Trump said.

The U.S. and Canada have traded tariffs on each other’s goods since late August, when Trump’s 50 percent levies on $27.6 billion worth of Canadian pr’oducts took effect.

Carney matched those tariffs in September, and Trump later banned American businesses from importing nearly $1 billion worth of Canadian dairy products, motor vehicles and many alcoholic beverages.

The president has also threatened to increase import taxes to 50 percent on Canadian cars, trucks, auto parts and steel starting on Jan. 1.

Carney said Sunday he had a “good conversation” with Trump on the “future” of trade between the two countries.

“This builds on our recent constructive discussions on the outlines of a mutually beneficial trade deal that would create jobs for our workers, boost affordability for families, and fully respect Canada’s languages, culture, and sovereignty,” the Canadian leader wrote on social platform X.

Carney added he and Trump’s teams “will now be working in the coming weeks to deliver that outcome.”

Trump also said Sunday the construction of the Keystone Pipeline expansion will be part of a trade agreement, noting Canada will pay for the project.

“We’re going to give them the route, and it’s largely been determined,” the president added.

The Biden administration revoked a federal permit for the Keystone XL project, which would expand the established pipeline between Western Canada and Texas. TC Energy canceled the expansion project in 2021.

Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said the project would benefit American farmers and ranchers in the form of lower diesel prices. Diesel costs nearly $6.30 per gallon as of Monday, per AAA.

Heading: Supreme court rules against Trump over bid to force California to set aside ballots
DNU Summary: The disputed ballots involve a Justice Department claim that about 20,000 non-citizens are on California’s voter rolls.
Body:
The supreme court on Monday ruled against the Trump administration and its attempts to force California election officials to segregate and not count ballots from people that the justice department claims are non-citizens. The ruling follows several lower courts siding with California officials, who argued the federal government was seeking to interfere in state elections.

California and the Trump administration have been in a legal standoff over the past few weeks following the justice department’s claim that 20,000 non-citizens were on the state’s voter rolls. The DoJ delivered a USB drive to Los Angeles and Sacramento election officials in mid-October with the names, giving only 48 hours for officials to review the list and threatening to sue if the ballots were not sequestered until those listed could verify their citizenship. Election officials refused, leading to a series of courtroom battles.

The justice department’s claims faced immediate pushback from state officials and voting rights groups, who questioned how the agency compiled the list and accused the Trump administration of a ploy to cast doubt over midterm elections. The justice department refused to provide details on its methodology and analysis from election officials found numerous suggestions the list contained inaccuracies.

“The Department of Justice has not provided the underlying evidence, source, or methodology supporting its assertions that individuals identified in its records are ineligible to vote,” Dean Logan, Los Angeles county clerk and recorder, said in a statement after receiving the list.

The fight between the Trump administration and California officials escalated over recent weeks and subsequent court rulings. The administration has threatened to prosecute election officials if they process ineligible non-citizen ballots, a move experts say would have no legal basis. The Trump administration has also opened a criminal investigation in California to pursue claims of non-citizen voting, as well as begun subpoenaing election officials.

US district judge David Carter previously rebuffed the administration’s request to segregate ballots in a ruling on 28 October. Carter, who was nominated to the bench by Bill Clinton, wrote in his decision about how the administration’s move to interfere in California’s vote was unusual and extreme.

“Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch,” Carter wrote.

The Trump administration’s demands are part of a larger effort by the federal government to assert a greater role in overseeing elections and push claims of voter fraud committed by non-citizens. The justice department has made a similar demand to segregate ballots in Washington state, while also filing criminal charges against 28 green card holders in California that the DoJ accuses of fraudulently registering to vote and casting illegal ballots.

Trump has also made vague promises to issue a $1m reward to anyone whose reports of voter fraud lead to an arrest or conviction. Data and experts have shown that ineligible non-citizen voting is extremely rare.

Heading: Trump to remove Rwanda and South Africa from US trade deal
DNU Summary: The removal would take effect in January 2027 under the African Growth and Opportunity Act.
Body:
US President Donald Trump has notified Congress of his intention to remove South Africa and Rwanda from a preferential trade programme, from 1 January 2027.

The African Growth and Opportunity Act (Agoa) allows eligible African countries to export thousands of products to the US duty-free.

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement that an annual review had found that both countries were engaging in practices inconsistent with the programme's eligibility requirements.

He added that the Trump administration had additionally notified the two countries of the decision.

The Trump administration cited barriers to US trade and investment, as well as concerns over national security and foreign policy interests in the region.

In Rwanda's case, Washington also raised concerns about human rights, political pluralism, the rule of law and workers' rights.

The move comes barely a week after Rwanda's defence ministry was hit with sanctions by US Treasury for its alleged role in the armed rebellion in eastern DR Congo.

The US Treasury said Rwanda's defence ministry directed thousands of troops to fight alongside M23 rebels in eastern DR Congo, providing weapons, equipment, logistics and training.

For South Africa, the US additionally pointed to corruption.

"The Trump administration is working to ensure our African partners take the necessary steps to meet the eligibility criteria," Greer said.

The announcement comes amid strained relations between Washington and both countries, with the proposed termination threatening their access to preferential trade arrangements with the US.

Last year, Trump accused South Africa of white genocide in a meeting with President Cyril Ramaphosa at the White House and launched a US refugee pathway for Afrikaners.

US Ambassador to South Africa Leo Brent Bozell III said it was regrettable that South African policies led to its termination from Agoa.

"This was a predictable and preventable outcome resulting from the rejection by South Africa's government of real concerns raised by the US," he wrote on X.

Heading: UN's peacekeeping mission in disputed Western Sahara ends after 35 years
DNU Summary: A smaller UN team is overseeing equipment removal after rival US and Russian resolutions failed in the Security Council.
Body:
FILE - A Sahrawi refugee boy stands in the shadow in the Boujdour refugee camp, Oct. 11, 2021. Bernat Armangue/AP hide caption

CASABLANCA, Morocco — The U.N.'s long-running peacekeeping mission for the disputed Western Sahara ceased operations Sunday after 35 years, as a result of a U.S.-Russia standoff at U.N. headquarters over the territory's future.

The end of the mission raises concerns about stability in the region. Rich in minerals and fisheries, Western Sahara is a vast desert territory roughly the size of Colorado along Africa's northwestern Atlantic coast. Once ruled by Spain, it is claimed by both Morocco and the pro-independence Polisario Front.

"This 1 November 2026 marks the start of the liquidation period," Stéphane Dujarric, spokesperson for the U.N. secretary general, said in a statement. "A smaller team reporting to the United Nations' Department of Operational Support will oversee the orderly transportation of assets belonging to troop-contributing countries to their respective nations, and the appropriate disposal of equipment belonging to the United Nations.''

The mission had been repeatedly extended since it was established in 1991. In the U.N. Security Council on Friday, Russia vetoed a draft U.S. resolution that would have supported Morocco's demand for sovereignty over Western Sahara and ended the peacekeeping mission next year.

Then a rival Russian resolution to extend the mission was voted down. The disagreement led to an abrupt end of the force's mandate.

Morocco's royal palace welcomed the non-renewal of the mission. It called it an "instrument to internationalize the dispute.''

The Polisario Front, backed by Algeria, called it "an unacceptable decision.'' The Algerian foreign ministry said it profoundly regrets the non-renewal of the mandate and criticized what it called the ''excessive bias'' of the U.S. draft resolution.

The U.N. classifies Western Sahara as a "non-self-governing territory," while critics of Morocco's control describe it as Africa's last colony. Morocco administers nearly all of the disputed territory, except for a narrow strip known as the "free zone" that lies east of a Moroccan-built sand wall.

After Morocco annexed it in 1975, the dispute escalated into an armed conflict that lasted more than 15 years and claimed more than 16,000 lives on both sides, according to the French Senate.

Bringing Western Sahara under its full sovereignty has been a central objective of Morocco's foreign policy for decades. Rabat, which has secured the backing of a growing number of Western capitals, including Washington, Paris and London, refers to the territory as its southern provinces. The dispute has become a defining feature of Morocco's diplomacy, with the kingdom often measuring its relations with other countries by their position on the issue.

The Polisario Front seeks independence for the territory, which it considers the homeland of the Indigenous Sahrawi people. Operating from refugee camps in the Algerian city of Tindouf, the movement aims to establish an independent Sahrawi Republic. Mainly backed by Algeria, Russia and South Africa, the Polisario has seen its international support dwindle in recent years.

A U.N.-brokered cease-fire took effect in 1991. The agreement also paved the way for the creation of the U.N. Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara, known as MINURSO.

The settlement plan provided for a referendum on self-determination, with independence among the options. But the vote never materialized. Morocco wanted the voter list to include Sahrawis living in the territory it controls, while the Polisario objected, arguing that their inclusion would tilt the outcome toward integration with Morocco. The movement insisted on using Spain's colonial census to determine voter eligibility.

Twenty MINURSO personnel lost their lives in the mission. The U.N. force was authorized to have 534 personnel, and its 2026-2027 budget was more than $62 million. The top military contributors to the force were Egypt, Ghana and Pakistan.

As the mission ends, the U.N. secretary-general ''calls upon all parties to respect and promote the rights of the people of Western Sahara,'' Dujarric said, and "remains concerned about the security situation throughout the Territory and the risk of escalation of hostilities. He calls on all concerned to exercise maximum restraint."

The Polisario withdrew from the ceasefire in 2020 after clashes and the territory has since remained the scene of tensions and low-intensity hostilities, the U.N. said last month.

Western Sahara is the major flashpoint in the rivalry between regional heavyweights Morocco and Algeria. Algiers, which arms, funds and hosts the Polisario Front, sees full Moroccan sovereignty over the territory as a major diplomatic defeat. The two countries severed diplomatic relations in 2021, and the end of the mission risks further straining ties and fueling an arms race.
